papers.what_it_is: A simulation study of fixed-point QAOA with three modifications (approximation-ratio objective, depth p = n with a two-parameter sin-cos schedule, Frobenius normalization) that finds a median shots-to-solution that does not grow with problem size up to 30 qubits.

existing.note: The paper states this in the abstract, Section IV and Section V. Detail the stored value omits: the text lists the three removals as alpha = 1, p = 8 and max-abs scaling (Section IV), while Section V lists them as AR targeting, normalization and the fixed low-dimensional parameterization. Figure 3 shows the removal of M1 or M2 gives a shallow exponential fit (about 1.06 to the power n) and only the M3 removal rises steeply; see the new figure assertion.

The metric is the shots-to-solution STS, defined as the reciprocal of the success probability P_alpha computed from the simulated state, so the 'median number of shots' is an expected shots figure computed from exact statevector probabilities, not a count of shots run. The decrease is of a median at one alpha (0.95); Figure 4 shows alpha = 1.0 rises with n.

assertions.value: The authors state that they introduce three modifications to the standard training procedure: targeting approximate rather than exact solutions through the success probability at a prescribed approximation ratio (M1), scaling the circuit depth linearly with the problem size using a sin-cos angle encoding (M2), and normalizing QUBO Hamiltonians by their Frobenius norm (M3).

assertions.value: The authors state that the procedure has a training stage, performed entirely classically with statevector simulation, and a sampling stage in which fixed pretrained parameters prepare the QAOA state on a quantum device with no further parameter optimization.

are directly used to prepare the QAOA state

assertions.value: The authors define the success probability P_alpha as the total probability of measuring a bitstring in the feasible set of approximation ratio alpha, with P at alpha = 1 equal to the probability of the exact minimum, and train the parameters to maximize the worst-case value of P at alpha = 0.95 over the training set.

papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that proves, for one-layer and two-layer QAOA with an oracle for the best angles, that the probability of finding the optimum of a constructed family of linear Ising models falls exponentially with size, and conjectures that this holds for every constant number of layers.

existing.note: The abstract states the broad conjecture, but the formal Conjecture 1 on p.9 is narrower: for each p there exists a linear Ising model with coefficient vector containing p + 1 different numbers whose optimum probability is below 1 for all angles. Combined with Theorem 1 this gives an exponential-runtime family of instances, not all linear functions. In the abstract, 'n' in 'p >= n' means the number of different coefficients; the body calls that m and uses n for the number of qubits.
existing.value: The authors state in the abstract that they conjecture QAOA needs exponential time to find the global optimum of linear functions for any constant value of p, with runtime linear only if p ≥ n, where n there is the number of different coefficients; the formal Conjecture 1 states only that for each p there is a linear Ising model whose coefficient vector contains p+1 different numbers for which, with p layers, the probability of measuring the optimal solution is below 1 for all angles.
quotes: We conjecture that QAOA needs exponential time to find the global optimum of linear functions for any constant value of p, and that the runtime is linear only if p ≥ n.

Conjecture 1. There is a linear Ising model with coefficients’ vector a containing p+1 different numbers such that the probability of measuring the optimal solution of the Ising model using the QAOA ansatz with p layers holds the inequality P r(a, γ, β) < 1 for all γ and β.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own conjecture, not proved beyond p = 2.

existing.note: The oracle assumption and the lower-bound statement are on p.5 in Section 3, not Section 2; the no-noise statement is in Section 4 on p.11. The runtime counted is the expected number of samples only.

The condition is on the existence of a, not on the angles. The runtime is the expected number of samples when an oracle supplies the best angles, and the exponential growth is for the constructed family of instances made by repeating the coefficient vector.
existing.value: The paper proves Theorem 1: for a constant number of QAOA layers p independent of the problem size n and a vector a of m positive real coefficients of a linear Ising model, if the probability of measuring the optimal solution is below 1 for all angle vectors of size p, then a family of linear Ising models can be built for which the QAOA runtime, counted as the average number of samples with an oracle supplying the best angles, grows exponentially with the problem size n.

RESULTS: Photonic probabilistic computer for image classification

papers.what_it_is: An MIT and Stanford experimental paper that builds a photonic probabilistic neuron from a bistable optical parametric oscillator seeded by vacuum noise, uses it with an FPGA or GPU for MNIST classification with a stochastic binary neural network and image generation with a pixelCNN, and estimates an all-optical platform.

existing.note: The demonstrated sampling rate is 10 kHz (Section Results, p.3).
existing.certainty_reason: The Discussion states this limit itself.

existing.note: The 96.5% is on 1,000 binarized images made by binarizing 100 grayscale MNIST test images 10 times each, with a network pre-trained in silico; the matrix-vector multiplications are done by the FPGA and the photonic element only samples the binary nodes. Diagonal counts in Figure 3(b) sum to about 965 of 1,000 for the experiment and about 970 for the simulation.
existing.value: The authors report an overall experimental classification accuracy of 96.5% for the optical stochastic binary neural network against 97.0% in numerical simulation, on 1,000 binarized images made by binarizing 100 grayscale MNIST test images 10 times each, with a network of 784 → 128 → 64 → 10 nodes pre-trained in silico whose matrix-vector multiplications are performed by the FPGA while the photonic neurons sample the binary node values.

A total of 1,000 binary images (100 grayscale testing images × 10 times of binarization = 1, 000 input images) are tested.
